chapters.title: 27. The End of Apartment No. 50
paragraphs: When Margarita reached the last words of the chapter, “...Thus did the fifth procurator of Judea, Pontius Pilate, greet the dawn of the fifteenth of Nisan,” morning had come.
In the little yard, in the branches of the willow and the linden, the sparrows could be heard carrying on a cheerful, excited morning conversation.

Margarita got up from the armchair, stretched, and only now felt how broken her body was and how badly she wanted to sleep. It is interesting to note that Margarita’s soul was in perfect order. Her thoughts were not in disarray; she was not in the least shaken by the fact that she had spent a supernatural night. She was not troubled by the memories of having been at Satan’s ball, of the master having been returned to her by some miracle, of the novel having risen from the ashes, of everything being back in its place again in the basement off the side street, from which the informer Aloisy Mogarych had been driven out. In short, her acquaintance with Woland had done her no psychological damage whatsoever. Everything was as though that was just how it ought to be.

She went into the next room, made sure that the master was sleeping soundly and peacefully, switched off the desk lamp that was no longer needed, and stretched out herself on the little sofa against the opposite wall, which was covered with an old torn sheet. A minute later she was asleep, and that morning she had no dreams at all. The rooms in the basement were silent, the developer’s whole little house was silent, and it was quiet in the secluded side street.

But at this time, that is, at dawn on Saturday, an entire floor in one of the Moscow institutions was not asleep, and its windows, which looked out onto a large asphalt-paved square that special machines were slowly driving around and cleaning with brushes, humming as they went, blazed with full light that cut through the light of the rising sun.
The whole floor was occupied by the investigation into the Woland case, and lamps had burned all night in ten offices.

Strictly speaking, the case had been clear since the day before, Friday, when the Variety had had to be closed owing to the disappearance of its management and all sorts of outrages that had taken place the evening before during the famous séance of black magic. But the point was that more and more new material kept arriving at the sleepless floor all the time, without a break.

Now the investigation into this strange case, which reeked quite unmistakably of devilry, and with an admixture of some sort of hypnotic tricks and quite distinct criminality besides, had the task of kneading all the diverse and tangled events that had taken place in different parts of Moscow into a single lump.
The first person who had to pay a visit to the sleepless floor, ablaze with electric light, was Arkady Apollonovich Sempleyarov, chairman of the Acoustics Commission.

After dinner on Friday the telephone rang in his apartment, located in a building by the Stone Bridge, and a man’s voice asked for Arkady Apollonovich. Arkady Apollonovich’s wife, who answered the telephone, replied gloomily that Arkady Apollonovich was unwell, had retired to rest, and could not come to the telephone. Nevertheless, Arkady Apollonovich did have to come to the telephone. To the question of who was asking for Arkady Apollonovich, the voice on the telephone very briefly said who.

“This very second... right away... this very minute...” babbled the usually very haughty wife of the chairman of the Acoustics Commission, and flew like an arrow into the bedroom to raise Arkady Apollonovich from the couch on which he lay, suffering hellish torments at the memory of yesterday’s séance and the nighttime scandal that had accompanied the expulsion of his niece from Saratov from the apartment.

True, not within a second, but not even within a minute either—within a quarter of a minute Arkady Apollonovich, with one slipper on his left foot and in nothing but his underwear, was already at the telephone, babbling into it:
“Yes, it’s me... I’m listening, I’m listening...”

His wife, who for these moments had forgotten all the vile crimes against fidelity of which the unfortunate Arkady Apollonovich had been convicted, kept poking her frightened face out of the corridor door, jabbing a slipper in the air and whispering:

“Put your slipper on, your slipper... You’ll catch cold in your feet,” to which Arkady Apollonovich, waving his wife away with his bare foot and making ferocious eyes at her, muttered into the telephone:
“Yes, yes, yes, of course, I understand... I’m leaving at once...”

Arkady Apollonovich spent the whole evening on that very floor where the investigation was being conducted. The conversation was painful, a most unpleasant conversation it was, for he had to tell, with the most complete frankness, not only about that vile séance and the fight in the box, but also, in passing, since it really was necessary, about Militsa Andreyevna Pokobatko of Elokhovskaya Street, and about the niece from Saratov, and about a great deal more, the telling of which caused Arkady Apollonovich inexpressible agonies.

It goes without saying that the testimony of Arkady Apollonovich, an intelligent and cultured man who had witnessed the disgraceful séance, a sensible and qualified witness who had given an excellent description both of the mysterious masked magician himself and of his two scoundrelly assistants, and who had remembered perfectly well that the magician’s name was precisely Woland, moved the investigation considerably forward. And comparing Arkady Apollonovich’s testimony with the testimony of others, among whom were certain ladies who had suffered after the séance (the one in violet underwear who had so shocked Rimsky, and, alas, many others), and the messenger Karpov, who had been sent to apartment No. 50 on Sadovaya Street, at once established, as a matter of fact, the place where the culprit behind all these adventures was to be sought.

Apartment No. 50 was visited, and more than once, and not only was it searched with extraordinary thoroughness, but its walls were tapped, its fireplace flues examined, and hiding places looked for. However, none of these measures produced any result, and on none of the visits to the apartment was anyone found in it, although it was perfectly clear that there was someone in the apartment—and this despite the fact that all the persons whose business it was, one way or another, to deal with questions concerning foreign performers arriving in Moscow firmly and categorically asserted that there was no black magician Woland in Moscow and could not possibly be.

He had positively not registered anywhere on arrival, had shown no one his passport or any other papers, contracts or agreements, and nobody had heard anything about him! Kitaitsev, head of the program department of the Entertainment Commission, swore by all that was holy that the vanished Styopa Likhodeyev had never sent him any program of a performance by any Woland for approval and had never telephoned Kitaitsev anything about the arrival of any such Woland. So that he, Kitaitsev, found it utterly incomprehensible and unknown how Styopa could have permitted such a séance at the Variety. And when they told him that Arkady Apollonovich had seen this magician at the séance with his own eyes, Kitaitsev merely spread his hands and raised his eyes to heaven. And from Kitaitsev’s eyes alone one could see, and boldly say, that he was as pure as crystal.
That same Prokhor Petrovich, chairman of the main Entertainment Commission...

Incidentally: he had returned to his suit immediately after the police entered his office, to the frenzied joy of Anna Richardovna and the great bewilderment of the needlessly disturbed police. Also incidentally: having returned to his place, in his gray striped suit, Prokhor Petrovich fully approved all the resolutions the suit had signed during his brief absence.
...so, as I was saying, that same Prokhor Petrovich most decidedly knew nothing about any Woland.

Something was emerging that was—say what you like—utterly preposterous: thousands of spectators, the entire staff of the Variety, and finally Sempleyarov, Arkady Apollonovich, a most highly educated man, had seen this magician, as well as his accursed assistants, and yet there was no way whatsoever of finding him anywhere. What, then, allow me to ask you, had he fallen through the earth right after his disgusting séance, or, as some maintain, had he never come to Moscow at all? But if one allows the first, then there is no doubt that, in falling through, he took the entire top management of the Variety along with him; and if the second, then does it not follow that the management of the ill-starred theater itself, having first committed some nasty trick (just remember the broken window in the office and the behavior of Ace of Diamonds!), had vanished from Moscow without a trace?

Justice must be done to whoever headed the investigation. The vanished Rimsky was tracked down with astonishing speed. It was only necessary to compare the behavior of Ace of Diamonds at the taxi stand by the cinema with certain times, such as when the séance had ended and when exactly Rimsky could have disappeared, in order to send a telegram to Leningrad at once. An hour later the answer came (toward Friday evening) that Rimsky had been found in room four hundred and twelve of the Astoria Hotel, on the fourth floor, next to the room where the repertory manager of one of the Moscow theaters then on tour in Leningrad was staying—that very room which, as everyone knows, has gray-blue furniture with gilt and a splendid bathroom.

Rimsky, discovered hiding in the wardrobe of room four hundred and twelve of the Astoria, was immediately arrested and questioned right there in Leningrad. After which a telegram came to Moscow informing them that the financial director of the Variety had turned out to be in a state of mental derangement, that he gave no sensible answers to questions, or did not wish to give any, and begged for only one thing: to be hidden in an armored cell and have an armed guard posted over him. From Moscow a telegram ordered that Rimsky be brought to Moscow under guard, as a result of which Rimsky left on Friday evening under such a guard on the evening train.

Toward Friday evening they also found Likhodeyev’s trail. Telegrams inquiring about Likhodeyev were sent out to every city, and an answer was received from Yalta that Likhodeyev had been in Yalta but had flown to Moscow by airplane.
The only one whose trail they could not pick up was Varenukha. The famous theater administrator, known to absolutely all of Moscow, had vanished without a trace, as if he had sunk into water.

Meanwhile they had to deal with incidents in other parts of Moscow as well, outside the Variety Theatre. They had to clear up the extraordinary case of the office workers singing “Glorious Sea” (incidentally: Professor Stravinsky managed to restore them to order within the space of two hours by means of some sort of injections under the skin), of persons presenting the devil knows what to other persons or institutions in the guise of money, and also of persons who had suffered from such presentations.

As goes without saying, the most unpleasant, the most scandalous and the most insoluble of all these cases was the case of the theft of the head of the late writer Berlioz straight out of the coffin in the hall at Griboyedov’s, carried out in broad daylight.
Twelve people were conducting the investigation, gathering up, as onto a knitting needle, the accursed loops of this complicated case, which were scattered all over Moscow.

One of the investigators arrived at Professor Stravinsky’s clinic and first of all asked to be shown a list of the persons who had been admitted to the clinic during the last three days. In this way Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy and the unfortunate master of ceremonies whose head had been torn off were discovered. They received little attention, however. By now it was easy to establish that these two had fallen victim to one and the same gang, headed by this mysterious magician. But Ivan Nikolayevich Bezdomny interested the investigator extremely.

The door of Ivanushka’s room, No. 117, opened toward evening on Friday, and into the room came a young, round-faced, calm man with a gentle manner, who looked nothing like an investigator and yet was one of the best investigators in Moscow. He saw, lying on the bed, a young man grown pale and drawn, with eyes in which a lack of interest in what was going on around him could be read, eyes that turned now somewhere into the distance, above his surroundings, now inward, into the young man himself.
The investigator introduced himself kindly and said he had dropped in on Ivan Nikolayevich to have a talk about the events at Patriarch’s Ponds the day before yesterday.

Oh, how Ivan would have triumphed if the investigator had come to him earlier, say, for instance, on the night before Thursday, when Ivan had been striving so violently and passionately to get people to listen to his story about Patriarch’s Ponds. Now his dream of helping to catch the consultant had come true; he no longer needed to run after anyone; they had come to him precisely to hear his tale of what had happened on Wednesday evening.

But, alas, Ivanushka had changed completely in the time that had passed since the moment of Berlioz’s death. He was ready to answer all the investigator’s questions willingly and politely, but indifference could be felt both in Ivan’s gaze and in his intonations. The fate of Berlioz no longer moved the poet.

Before the investigator came, Ivanushka had been dozing as he lay there, and certain visions had passed before him. Thus he had seen a city, strange, incomprehensible, nonexistent, with blocks of marble, worn colonnades, roofs glittering in the sun, the black, gloomy and merciless Antonia Tower, the palace on the western hill sunk almost to its roofs in the tropical greenery of a garden, bronze statues burning in the sunset above that greenery; he had seen Roman centuries, clad in armor, marching beneath the walls of the ancient city.

In his drowsiness there appeared before Ivan a man sitting motionless in an armchair, clean-shaven, with a tormented yellow face, a man in a white mantle with a red lining, gazing with hatred into a lush and alien garden. Ivan also saw a treeless yellow hill with emptied posts and crossbeams.
But what had happened at Patriarch’s Ponds no longer interested the poet Ivan Bezdomny.
“Tell me, Ivan Nikolayevich, how far were you yourself from the turnstile when Berlioz fell under the tram?”
A barely noticeable, indifferent smile for some reason touched Ivan’s lips, and he replied:
“I was far away.”
“And that checkered fellow was right by the turnstile?”
“No, he was sitting on a bench not far off.”
“You remember clearly that he did not go up to the turnstile at the moment Berlioz fell?”
“I remember. He didn’t. He was sitting sprawled out.”

These questions were the investigator’s last. After them he stood up, held out his hand to Ivanushka, wished him a speedy recovery, and expressed the hope that soon he would again be reading his poems.
“No,” Ivan replied quietly, “I will not write any more poems.”
The investigator smiled politely and permitted himself to express his confidence that the poet was at present in a state of some depression, but that it would soon pass.
“No,” responded Ivan, looking not at the investigator but into the distance, at the fading sky, “this will never pass for me. The poems I wrote were bad poems, and now I have understood that.”

The investigator left Ivanushka having obtained some very important material. By following the thread of events from the end back to the beginning, they had finally managed to reach the source from which all the events had flowed. The investigator had no doubt that these events had begun with the murder at Patriarch’s. Of course, neither Ivanushka nor that checkered fellow had pushed the unfortunate chairman of Massolit under the tram; physically, so to speak, no one had contributed to his fall under the wheels. But the investigator was sure that Berlioz had thrown himself under the tram (or fallen under it) while hypnotized.

Yes, there was a great deal of material now, and it was already known whom to catch and where. But the whole point was that catching them was impossible by any means. In the thrice-accursed apartment No. 50 there was undoubtedly, it must be repeated, someone. From time to time this apartment answered telephone calls in a voice that was now crackling, now nasal; sometimes a window in the apartment was opened; what is more, the sounds of a gramophone could be heard coming from it. And yet every time anyone went there, there turned out to be absolutely no one in it. And they had been there more than once already, and at different times of day and night. And that was not all: they had gone through the apartment with a net, checking every corner. The apartment had long been under suspicion. They guarded not only the way that led into the yard through the gateway, but the back entrance as well; and that was not all: a guard had been posted on the roof by the chimneys. Yes, apartment No. 50 was playing pranks, and nothing could be done about it.

So matters dragged on until midnight between Friday and Saturday, when Baron Meigel, dressed in evening clothes and patent-leather shoes, solemnly proceeded into apartment No. 50 as a guest. The baron could be heard being let into the apartment. Exactly ten minutes after that, without any ringing, the apartment was visited, but not only were the hosts not found in it, but, what was quite bizarre, no trace of Baron Meigel was discovered in it either.

So then, as has been said, matters dragged on in this way until Saturday’s dawn. Here new and very interesting data were added. A six-seat passenger plane flying in from the Crimea landed at the Moscow airfield. Among the other passengers, one strange passenger got off. This was a young citizen, wildly overgrown with stubble, who had not washed for about three days, with inflamed and frightened eyes, without luggage and dressed somewhat fancifully. The citizen wore a tall sheepskin hat, a felt Caucasian cloak over a nightshirt, and new blue leather bedroom slippers, just purchased. As soon as he stepped away from the little ladder by which people descended from the plane’s cabin, he was approached. This citizen had been expected, and some time later the unforgettable director of the Variety, Stepan Bogdanovich Likhodeyev, appeared before the investigation. He added new data. It now became clear that Woland had penetrated the Variety in the guise of a performer, having hypnotized Styopa Likhodeyev, and had then contrived to throw that same Styopa out of Moscow to God knows how many kilometers away. The material had thus increased, but this did not make things any easier; rather, it made them, perhaps, even a tiny bit harder, for it was becoming obvious that getting hold of a personage capable of tricks like the one to which Stepan Bogdanovich had fallen victim would not be so very easy. Incidentally, Likhodeyev, at his own request, was confined in a secure cell, and there appeared before the investigation Varenukha, just arrested in his apartment, to which he had returned after an unexplained absence of almost two days.

Despite the promise he had given Azazello not to lie anymore, the administrator began precisely with a lie. Though, for that matter, he cannot be judged very harshly for it. After all, Azazello had forbidden him to lie and be rude on the telephone, and in this instance the administrator was talking without the aid of that device. With shifting eyes, Ivan Savelyevich declared that on Thursday afternoon he had got drunk all by himself in his office at the Variety, after which he had gone somewhere, but where he did not remember, had drunk some starka somewhere else, but where he did not remember, had lain about under a fence somewhere, but where, once again, he did not remember. Only after the administrator was told that by his stupid and reckless behavior he was hindering the investigation of an important case and would, of course, be held answerable for it, did Varenukha burst into sobs and, looking around him, whisper in a trembling voice that he was lying solely out of fear, afraid of the revenge of Woland’s gang, in whose hands he had already been, and that he asked, begged, longed to be locked in an armored cell.
“Pah, the devil! What is it with them and this armored cell!” grumbled one of those conducting the investigation.
“Those scoundrels have given them a bad fright,” said the investigator who had visited Ivanushka.

They calmed Varenukha as best they could, told him he would be protected even without any cell, and then it came out that he had not drunk any starka under a fence, but that he had been beaten by two men, one red-haired with a fang, and the other a fat fellow...
“Ah, resembling a cat?”

“Yes, yes, yes,” whispered the administrator, faint with fear and looking around every second, and he laid out further details of how he had existed for about two days in apartment No. 50 as a vampire-spotter who had very nearly caused the death of the financial director Rimsky...

At this point Rimsky, brought in on the Leningrad train, was led in. However, this gray-haired old man, trembling with fear and mentally deranged, in whom it was very hard to recognize the former financial director, would not tell the truth for anything, and proved very stubborn in this respect. Rimsky maintained that he had not seen any Hella at the window of his office at night, nor any Varenukha, but that he had simply felt unwell and in a state of unconsciousness had left for Leningrad. Needless to say, the sick financial director concluded his testimony with a request to be confined in an armored cell.

Annushka was arrested while making an attempt to hand a ten-dollar bill to the cashier of a department store on the Arbat. Annushka’s story about people flying out of the window of the building on Sadovaya and about the little horseshoe which, according to her, Annushka had picked up in order to hand it in to the police, was listened to attentively.
“Was the horseshoe really gold with diamonds?” they asked Annushka.
“As if I don’t know diamonds,” Annushka replied.
“But what he gave you was tenners, so you say?”
“As if I don’t know tenners,” Annushka replied.
“Well, and when did they turn into dollars?”

“I don’t know anything about any dollars, and I never saw any dollars,” Annushka replied shrilly. “We’re within our rights! We were given a reward, we’re buying calico with it...” and here she started talking a lot of nonsense about how she was not answerable for the house management, which had let unclean powers settle on the fifth floor, so there was no living with them.

At this point the investigator waved his pen at Annushka, because she had thoroughly bored everyone, and wrote her out a pass to leave on a green slip of paper, after which, to the general satisfaction, Annushka disappeared from the building.

Then a whole string of people followed one after another, and among them was Nikolai Ivanovich, just arrested solely because of the stupidity of his jealous wife, who toward morning had informed the police that her husband was missing. Nikolai Ivanovich did not greatly surprise the investigation when he laid on the table a clownish certificate stating that he had spent the time at Satan’s ball. In his stories of how he had carried Margarita Nikolayevna’s naked housemaid through the air on his back to go bathing in a river somewhere at the devil’s own back of beyond, and of the naked Margarita Nikolayevna’s appearance at the window that had preceded this, Nikolai Ivanovich departed somewhat from the truth. Thus, for instance, he did not consider it necessary to mention that he had come into the bedroom with the discarded slip in his hands and that he had called Natasha Venus. According to his account, Natasha had flown out of the window, mounted him, and dragged him off out of Moscow...
“Yielding to force, I was compelled to submit,” Nikolai Ivanovich related, and he concluded his tall tales with a request that not a word of this be communicated to his wife. Which was promised him.
Nikolai Ivanovich’s testimony made it possible to establish that Margarita Nikolayevna, as well as her housemaid Natasha, had disappeared without any trace. Measures were taken to find them.

Thus was the morning of Saturday marked by an investigation that did not stop for a second. In the city at this time quite impossible rumors kept arising and spreading, in which a tiny share of truth was embellished with the most luxuriant lies. People said that there had been a séance at the Variety after which all two thousand spectators had run out into the street as naked as the day they were born; that a printing works of counterfeit magic papers had been raided on Sadovaya Street; that some gang had kidnapped five heads of departments in the entertainment sector, but that the police had found them all at once; and a great deal more that one does not even want to repeat.

Meanwhile it was getting on toward lunchtime, and then, where the investigation was being conducted, the telephone rang. It was a report from Sadovaya that the accursed apartment had again shown signs of life. It was said that its windows had been opened from inside, that the sounds of a piano and singing had come from it, and that a black cat had been seen in the window, sitting on the sill and basking in the sun.

At about four o’clock on that hot afternoon a large party of men in civilian clothes got out of three cars a short distance before building No. 302-bis on Sadovaya Street. Here the large group that had arrived split into two small ones, one of which went through the gateway of the building and across the yard straight to entrance six, while the other opened the small, usually boarded-up door that led to the back stairs, and both began climbing by different staircases to apartment No. 50.

At this time Koroviev and Azazello—Koroviev in his usual outfit, and not at all in his festive tailcoat—were sitting in the dining room of the apartment, finishing their breakfast. Woland, as was his custom, was in the bedroom, and where the cat was, nobody knew. But judging by the clatter of saucepans coming from the kitchen, one could assume that Behemoth was there precisely, playing the fool, as was his custom.
“And what are those footsteps on the stairs?” asked Koroviev, toying with a spoon in his cup of black coffee.
“Oh, that’s them coming to arrest us,” answered Azazello, and drank a little glass of cognac.
“Ah, well, well,” Koroviev answered to that.

Those coming up the front staircase were meanwhile already on the third-floor landing. There two plumbers of some sort were fiddling with the radiator of the steam heating. The newcomers exchanged a meaningful look with the plumbers.
“They’re all home,” whispered one of the plumbers, tapping on the pipe with a hammer.

Then the one in front openly took a black Mauser out from under his coat, and another, beside him, a set of lock picks. In general, those going to apartment No. 50 were properly equipped. Two of them had in their pockets thin silk nets that unfolded easily. Another had a lasso, another had gauze masks and ampoules of chloroform.

In one second the front door of apartment No. 50 was opened, and all the visitors found themselves in the front hall, while a door banging in the kitchen at that moment showed that the second group had also arrived from the back stairs in good time.

This time, if not complete success, then at least some sort of success was evident. The men instantly scattered through all the rooms and found no one anywhere, but on the other hand in the dining room they discovered the remains of a breakfast that had evidently only just been abandoned, and in the living room, on the mantelpiece, beside a crystal jug, sat an enormous black cat. He was holding a Primus stove in his paws.
In complete silence those who had entered the living room contemplated this cat for quite a long time.
“M-yes... really something...” whispered one of the newcomers.

“I’m not making mischief, I’m not bothering anyone, I’m fixing the Primus,” the cat said, frowning in an unfriendly way, “and I further consider it my duty to warn you that the cat is an ancient and inviolable animal.”
“An exceptionally clean job,” whispered one of those who had entered, and another said loudly and distinctly:
“Well, sir, inviolable ventriloquist cat, kindly step this way!”
A silk net unfolded and flew up, but the man who threw it, to everyone’s complete astonishment, missed and caught only the jug, which at once smashed with a ringing crash.

“Missed the contract!” yelled the cat. “Hurrah!” And here, setting the Primus aside, he whipped a Browning from behind his back. In a flash he aimed it at the man standing nearest him, but before the cat could fire, fire blazed in that man’s hand, and with the shot from the Mauser the cat flopped head first from the mantelpiece to the floor, dropping the Browning and letting go of the Primus.

“It’s all over,” said the cat in a weak voice, and sprawled languidly in a pool of blood. “Step away from me for a second, let me say farewell to the earth. O my friend Azazello!” moaned the cat, bleeding profusely. “Where are you?” The cat rolled his dimming eyes toward the dining room door. “You did not come to my aid at the moment of unequal combat. You abandoned poor Behemoth, trading him for a glass of—very good, admittedly—cognac! Well, then, let my death lie on your conscience, and I bequeath you my Browning...”
“The net, the net, the net,” they whispered anxiously around the cat. But the net, the devil knows why, got caught in somebody’s pocket and would not come out.

“The only thing that can save a mortally wounded cat,” said the cat, “is a swig of gasoline...” and, taking advantage of the confusion, he put his mouth to the round opening in the Primus and drank his fill of gasoline. At once the blood stopped flowing from under his upper left paw. The cat leaped up alive and lively, grabbed the Primus under his arm, sprang with it back onto the mantelpiece, and from there, tearing the wallpaper, climbed up the wall, and in about two seconds was sitting high above the newcomers on the metal curtain rod.

In an instant hands seized the curtain and tore it down together with the rod, so that sunlight poured into the shaded room. But neither the fraudulently recovered cat nor the Primus fell down. The cat, without parting from the Primus, managed to swing through the air and leap onto the chandelier that hung in the center of the room.
“A stepladder!” someone shouted from below.

“I challenge you to a duel!” bawled the cat, flying over their heads on the swinging chandelier, and here the Browning was in his paws again, while he lodged the Primus between the branches of the chandelier. The cat took aim and, flying like a pendulum over the heads of the newcomers, opened fire on them. The din shook the apartment. Crystal fragments from the chandelier showered onto the floor, the mirror over the mantelpiece cracked into stars, plaster dust flew, spent cartridge cases bounced across the floor, the windowpanes burst, gasoline began to spurt from the shot-through Primus. Now there could be no question of taking the cat alive, and the newcomers fired back at him furiously and accurately from their Mausers, at his head, his belly, his chest and his back. The shooting caused panic on the asphalt in the yard.

But this shooting lasted a very short time and began to die down of its own accord. The thing was that it had done no harm either to the cat or to the newcomers. Not only was no one killed, no one was even wounded; everyone, including the cat, remained completely unharmed. One of the newcomers, to check this conclusively, fired five or so shots at the accursed animal’s head, and the cat briskly answered with a whole clip. And again the same thing: it made no impression on anyone. The cat swayed in the chandelier, whose swings were growing smaller and smaller, blowing for some reason into the muzzle of the Browning and spitting on his paw. On the faces of those standing silently below appeared an expression of utter bewilderment. This was the only case, or one of the only cases, in which shooting turned out to be completely ineffective. One might, of course, suppose that the cat’s Browning was some sort of toy, but that could by no means be said of the newcomers’ Mausers. As for the cat’s first wound, there was clearly not the slightest doubt that it had been nothing but a trick and swinish pretense, as had the drinking of the gasoline.

One more attempt was made to get the cat. A lasso was thrown; it caught on one of the candles, and the chandelier came crashing down. Its impact seemed to shake the whole block of the building, but nothing came of it. Those present were showered with fragments, while the cat flew through the air and settled high up under the ceiling on the top of the gilded frame of the mirror over the mantelpiece. He had no intention of running off anywhere and even, on the contrary, sitting in comparative safety, launched into another speech.
“I utterly fail to understand,” he said from above, “the reasons for such harsh treatment of me...”
And here this speech was interrupted at its very beginning by a heavy, low voice heard from no one knew where:
“What is going on in the apartment? I am being prevented from working.”
Another voice, unpleasant and nasal, responded:
“Well, Behemoth, of course, the devil take him!”
A third, quavering voice said:
“Messire! Saturday. The sun is going down. It is time for us to go.”

“Excuse me, I cannot converse any longer,” said the cat from the mirror. “It is time for us to go.” He flung his Browning and knocked out both panes in the window. Then he splashed gasoline down below, and the gasoline burst into flame of its own accord, throwing a wave of fire right up to the ceiling.

It caught fire somehow unusually fast and fiercely, as does not happen even with gasoline. At once the wallpaper began to smoke, the torn-down curtain on the floor caught fire, and the frames of the broken windows began to smolder. The cat coiled like a spring, meowed, sprang from the mirror to the windowsill and vanished beyond it together with his Primus. Shots rang out outside. A man sitting on the iron fire escape at the level of the jeweler’s widow’s windows fired at the cat as he flew from windowsill to windowsill, making for the corner drainpipe of the building, which, as has been said, was built in the shape of a U. Up this pipe the cat climbed onto the roof. There, unfortunately also without result, he was fired at by the guard watching the chimneys, and the cat made off into the setting sun that was flooding the city.

At this time in the apartment the parquet floor flared up under the newcomers’ feet, and in the fire, on the spot where the cat had lain with his pretended wound, there appeared, growing denser and denser, the corpse of the former Baron Meigel, with his chin jutting upward and glassy eyes. It was no longer possible to drag him out.

Hopping over the burning squares of parquet, slapping their palms on their smoking shoulders and chests, those who had been in the living room retreated into the study and the front hall. Those who had been in the dining room and the bedroom ran out through the corridor. Those who had been in the kitchen came running too and rushed into the front hall. The living room was already full of fire and smoke. Someone, on the run, managed to dial the number of the fire brigade and shout briefly into the receiver:
“Sadovaya, three-oh-two-bis!”
It was impossible to stay any longer. The flames lashed out into the front hall. It became hard to breathe.
As soon as the first wisps of smoke came puffing out of the broken windows of the bewitched apartment, desperate human cries rang out in the yard:
“Fire! Fire! We’re burning!”
In various apartments of the building people began shouting into telephones:
“Sadovaya! Sadovaya, three-oh-two-bis!”

While on Sadovaya there sounded the heart-stopping clang of bells on the long red engines racing in from every part of the city, the people rushing about the yard saw three dark silhouettes, men’s silhouettes as it seemed, and one silhouette of a naked woman fly out of a fifth-floor window together with the smoke.

chapters.title: 28. The Last Adventures of Koroviev and Behemoth
paragraphs: Whether these silhouettes were real, or whether they only seemed so to the fear-stricken tenants of the ill-starred building on Sadovaya, of course cannot be said with certainty. If they were real, nobody knows either where exactly they went. Nor can we say where they separated, but we do know that about a quarter of an hour after the fire on Sadovaya began, a tall citizen in a checkered suit, and with him a large black cat, appeared at the mirrored doors of the Torgsin store at Smolensky Market.
Deftly weaving among the passersby, the citizen opened the outer door of the store. But here a small, bony and extremely ill-disposed doorman barred his way and said irritably:
“No cats allowed!”
“I beg your pardon,” quavered the tall one, cupping a knobby hand to his ear like someone hard of hearing, “cats, you say? But where do you see a cat?”

The doorman’s eyes bulged, and with good reason: there was no longer any cat at the citizen’s feet; instead, a fat fellow in a torn cap, whose mug did indeed slightly resemble a cat’s, was already poking out from behind his shoulder and pushing to get into the store. In the fat fellow’s hands was a Primus stove.
For some reason this pair of customers did not appeal to the misanthropic doorman.
“We take foreign currency only,” he wheezed, looking irritably from under his shaggy gray eyebrows, which seemed moth-eaten.

“My dear fellow,” quavered the tall one, his eye flashing from his broken pince-nez, “and how do you know that I haven’t got any? Are you judging by my suit? Never do that, most precious guardian! You may be mistaken, and very greatly mistaken at that. Reread, if nothing else, the story of the famous caliph Harun al-Rashid. But in the present case, setting that story aside for the time being, I want to tell you that I will complain about you to the manager and tell him such things about you that you might not have to leave your post between the gleaming mirrored doors.”
“For all you know, I’ve got a whole Primus full of currency,” the catlike fat fellow, who kept shoving his way into the store, hotly butted into the conversation.

Behind them the public was already pressing forward and getting angry. Looking at the outlandish pair with hatred and doubt, the doorman stepped aside, and our acquaintances, Koroviev and Behemoth, found themselves inside the store. Here, first of all, they looked around, and then, in a ringing voice that could be heard in absolutely every corner, Koroviev announced:
“A splendid store! A very, very good store!”
The public at the counters turned around and for some reason looked at the speaker in amazement, although he had every reason to praise the store.

Hundreds of bolts of calico in the richest colors could be seen in the pigeonholes of the shelves. Behind them were piled muslins and chiffons and tailcoat broadcloth. Whole stacks of shoeboxes receded into the distance, and several women citizens sat on low little chairs, their right foot in an old, worn-out shoe and their left in a new, gleaming pump, which they tapped on the little rug with a preoccupied air. Somewhere in the depths, around a corner, gramophones sang and played.

But, passing by all these delights, Koroviev and Behemoth headed straight for the junction of the delicatessen and confectionery departments. Here there was plenty of room; the women citizens in headscarves and little berets were not pressing against the counters as in the calico department.

A short, perfectly square man, shaven blue, in horn-rimmed glasses, in a brand-new hat that was not crumpled and had no stains on its band, in a lilac coat and russet kid gloves, stood at the counter, imperiously lowing something. A salesman in a clean white smock and a blue cap was serving the lilac customer. With a very sharp knife, very like the knife stolen by Levi Matvei, he was removing from a fat, weeping pink salmon its snakelike skin with a silvery sheen.
“This department is magnificent too,” Koroviev solemnly acknowledged, “and the foreigner is a nice one,” and he pointed a benevolent finger at the lilac back.
“No, Fagot, no,” Behemoth replied pensively, “you’re mistaken, my dear chap. Something is lacking in the lilac gentleman’s face, in my opinion.”
The lilac back gave a start, but probably by chance, for the foreigner could not have understood what Koroviev and his companion were saying in Russian.
“Is goot?” the lilac customer asked sternly.
“World-class!” the salesman replied, coquettishly picking under the skin with the point of his knife.
“Goot I like, bad—no,” the foreigner said severely.
“But of course!” the salesman replied rapturously.
At this point our acquaintances moved away from the foreigner and his salmon to the end of the confectionery counter.
“It’s hot today,” Koroviev said, addressing a young, red-cheeked salesgirl, and received no answer from her to this. “How much are the tangerines?” Koroviev then inquired of her.
“Thirty kopecks a kilo,” the salesgirl replied.
“Everything bites,” Koroviev observed with a sigh. “Ah, me, ah, me...” He thought a little more and invited his companion: “Eat up, Behemoth.”
The fat fellow put his Primus under his arm, took possession of the top tangerine in the pyramid, and, having gobbled it up right there, peel and all, started on a second.
The salesgirl was seized with mortal terror.
“You’re out of your mind!” she cried, losing her rosy color. “Give me your receipt! Your receipt!” And she dropped the candy tongs.

“Darling, sweetheart, my beauty,” Koroviev wheezed, leaning across the counter and winking at the salesgirl, “we’re out of currency today... well, what can you do! But I swear to you, the very next time, and no later than Monday, we’ll pay it all back in hard cash! We’re not far from here, on Sadovaya, where the fire is...”

Behemoth, having swallowed a third tangerine, stuck his paw into an ingenious structure of chocolate bars, pulled out one at the bottom, at which, of course, the whole thing collapsed, and swallowed it together with its gold wrapper.

The salesmen behind the fish counter stood as if turned to stone, knives in hand; the lilac foreigner turned toward the robbers, and here it at once became clear that Behemoth was wrong: it was not that something was lacking in the lilac man’s face, but rather, on the contrary, that there was something extra in it—hanging cheeks and shifty eyes.
Turning completely yellow, the salesgirl cried out wretchedly to the whole store:
“Palosich! Palosich!”

The public from the calico department came pouring toward this cry, while Behemoth moved away from the confectionery temptations and thrust his paw into a barrel labeled “Choice Kerch Herring,” pulled out a couple of herrings and swallowed them, spitting out the tails.
“Palosich!” came the desperate cry again from behind the confectionery counter, and from behind the fish counter a salesman with a goatee barked:
“What do you think you’re doing, you vermin?!”

Pavel Iosifovich was already hurrying to the scene of action. He was an imposing man in a clean white smock, like a surgeon, with a pencil sticking out of his pocket. Pavel Iosifovich was evidently an experienced man. Seeing the tail of the third herring in Behemoth’s mouth, he assessed the situation in an instant, understood absolutely everything, and, without entering into any argument with the brazen pair, waved his hand toward the street, commanding:
“Whistle!”
The doorman shot out of the mirrored doors onto the corner of Smolensky and burst into an ominous whistling. The public began to surround the scoundrels, and then Koroviev entered the fray.

“Citizens!” he cried in a thin, vibrating voice. “What is going on here? Eh? Allow me to ask you that! A poor man”—Koroviev let a tremor into his voice and pointed to Behemoth, who immediately put on a tearful face—“a poor man spends all day fixing Primus stoves; he got hungry... and where is he supposed to get foreign currency?”
Pavel Iosifovich, usually reserved and calm, shouted sternly at this:
“You drop that!” and waved toward the street, impatiently now. Then the trills by the door rang out more merrily.
But Koroviev, not put off by Pavel Iosifovich’s outburst, went on:

“Where from?—I put that question to you all! He is exhausted with hunger and thirst! He is hot. So the poor wretch took a tangerine to try. And the whole price of that tangerine is three kopecks. And there they go, whistling like nightingales in the woods in springtime, disturbing the police, taking them away from their work. But he’s allowed? Eh?” And here Koroviev pointed at the lilac fat man, at which the most violent alarm showed on the latter’s face. “Who is he? Eh? Where has he come from? What for? Were we pining without him, or something? Did we invite him, or something? Of course,” the former choirmaster bellowed at the top of his voice, twisting his mouth sarcastically, “he, you see, is in a smart lilac suit, all swollen up with salmon, he’s stuffed full of currency, but what about our fellow, what about ours?! It’s bitter for me! Bitter! Bitter!” howled Koroviev, like the best man at an old-fashioned wedding.

This whole extremely stupid, tactless and probably politically harmful speech made Pavel Iosifovich shake with anger, but, strange as it may seem, one could tell from the eyes of the crowding public that it had aroused sympathy in a great many people! And when Behemoth, putting his dirty, torn sleeve to his eye, exclaimed tragically:

“Thank you, faithful friend, for standing up for the victim!”—a miracle occurred. A most respectable, quiet little old man, poorly but neatly dressed, a little old man who was buying three almond pastries in the confectionery department, was suddenly transformed. His eyes flashed with martial fire, he turned crimson, flung the little bag of pastries to the floor and cried:

“It’s true!” in a thin, childish voice. Then he snatched up a tray, throwing off it the remains of the chocolate Eiffel Tower that Behemoth had wrecked, brandished it, with his left hand tore the hat off the foreigner, and with his right struck the foreigner a full swing with the flat of the tray on his bald head. There rolled out a sound such as one hears when sheet iron is thrown off a truck onto the ground. The fat man, turning white, toppled over backward and sat down in the tub of Kerch herring, sending up a fountain of herring brine. At once a second miracle took place. The lilac man, having sunk into the tub, cried out in pure Russian, without a trace of any accent:
“Murder! Police! Bandits are murdering me!”—evidently, as a result of the shock, having suddenly mastered a language until then unknown to him.

Then the doorman’s whistling stopped, and among the crowds of agitated shoppers two police helmets flashed into view, approaching. But the treacherous Behemoth, the way one sloshes a bench in a bathhouse from a washtub, sloshed the confectionery counter with gasoline from the Primus, and it burst into flame of its own accord. The flames shot upward and ran along the counter, devouring the pretty paper ribbons on the fruit baskets. The salesgirls rushed squealing from behind the counter, and no sooner had they leaped out from behind it than the linen blinds on the windows burst into flame and the gasoline on the floor caught fire. The public, at once raising a desperate cry, recoiled from the confectionery department, trampling the no longer needed Pavel Iosifovich, while from behind the fish counter the salesmen with their sharpened knives trotted in single file toward the back door. The lilac citizen, tearing himself out of the tub, all covered in herring slop, rolled over the salmon on the counter and followed them. The glass in the mirrored exit doors, pushed out by people trying to save themselves, rang and fell in showers, while both scoundrels, Koroviev and the glutton Behemoth, disappeared somewhere, and where, no one could make out. Later on, eyewitnesses who had been present at the start of the fire in the Torgsin at Smolensky related that the two hooligans had supposedly flown up to the ceiling and there had supposedly both burst like children’s balloons. It is doubtful, of course, that things happened exactly like that, but what we do not know, we do not know.

But we do know that exactly one minute after the incident at Smolensky, Behemoth and Koroviev were already on the sidewalk of the boulevard, right by the house of Griboyedov’s aunt. Koroviev stopped by the railing and began to speak:

“Bah! But this is the writers’ house! You know, Behemoth, I have heard a great many good and flattering things about this house. Pay attention to this house, my friend. It is pleasant to think that under this roof a whole abyss of talents is hidden away and ripening.”
“Like pineapples in hothouses,” said Behemoth, and, to admire the cream-colored house with the columns better, he climbed up onto the concrete base of the cast-iron railing.

“Perfectly true,” Koroviev agreed with his inseparable companion, “and a sweet dread rolls up to one’s heart when one thinks that in this house the future author of Don Quixote, or Faust, or, the devil take me, Dead Souls, is ripening at this very moment! Eh?”
“Frightening to think of,” Behemoth confirmed.

“Yes,” Koroviev went on, “astonishing things may be expected from the hotbeds of this house, which has united under its roof several thousand ascetics who have resolved to devote their lives selflessly to the service of Melpomene, Polyhymnia and Thalia. Can you imagine what a stir there will be when one of them, for a start, presents the reading public with The Inspector General, or, at the very worst, Eugene Onegin!”
“Easy as anything,” Behemoth again confirmed.

“Yes,” Koroviev went on, and raised a worried finger, “but! But, I say, and I repeat it—but! Provided these tender hothouse plants are not attacked by some microorganism, are not eaten away at the root, provided they do not rot! And that does happen to pineapples! Oh, oh, oh, how it happens!”
“By the way,” inquired Behemoth, poking his round head through a gap in the railing, “what are they doing on the veranda?”

“Having dinner,” Koroviev explained. “I will add, my dear, that there is a very decent and inexpensive restaurant here. And I, meanwhile, like any tourist before continuing his journey, feel a desire to have a bite and drink a big ice-cold mug of beer.”
“Me too,” Behemoth answered, and both scoundrels strode along the asphalt path under the lindens straight toward the veranda of the restaurant, which sensed no trouble.

A pale and bored woman citizen in white ankle socks and a little white beret with a little tail was sitting on a bentwood chair at the corner entrance to the veranda, where an opening had been made in the greenery of the trellis. In front of her, on a plain kitchen table, lay a thick ledger of the office type, in which, for reasons unknown, the citizen wrote down the names of those entering the restaurant. It was precisely this citizen who stopped Koroviev and Behemoth.
“Your membership cards?” She was looking with surprise at Koroviev’s pince-nez, and also at Behemoth’s Primus and Behemoth’s torn elbow.
“I offer you a thousand apologies, what membership cards?” asked Koroviev, surprised.
“Are you writers?” the citizen asked in her turn.
“Unquestionably,” Koroviev answered with dignity.
“Your membership cards?” the citizen repeated.
“My lovely...” Koroviev began tenderly.
“I am not your lovely,” the citizen interrupted him.

“Oh, what a pity,” Koroviev said, disappointed, and went on: “Well, then, if you do not care to be lovely, which would be most pleasant, you need not be. So then: to make sure that Dostoevsky is a writer, would one really have to ask him for his membership card? Why, take any five pages from any one of his novels, and without any card you will be convinced that you are dealing with a writer. Indeed, I suppose he never had any card at all! What do you think?” Koroviev turned to Behemoth.
“I’ll bet he didn’t,” the latter replied, setting the Primus on the table beside the ledger and wiping the sweat from his sooty forehead with his hand.
“You are not Dostoevsky,” said the citizen, whom Koroviev was confusing.
“Well, who can tell, who can tell,” he replied.
“Dostoevsky is dead,” said the citizen, but somehow not very confidently.
“I protest!” Behemoth exclaimed hotly. “Dostoevsky is immortal!”
“Your membership cards, citizens,” said the citizen.

“For pity’s sake, this is ridiculous, after all,” Koroviev would not give up. “A writer is not defined by a membership card at all, but by what he writes! How do you know what ideas are swarming in my head? Or in this head?” And he pointed to Behemoth’s head, from which the latter at once removed his cap, as if so that the citizen could examine it better.
“Let people through, citizens,” she said, nervous by now.

Koroviev and Behemoth stepped aside and let through some writer in a gray suit and a tieless white summer shirt, whose collar lay spread wide over the collar of his jacket, with a newspaper under his arm. The writer nodded affably to the citizen, put some squiggle in the ledger held out to him as he went by, and proceeded onto the veranda.

“Alas, not for us, not for us,” Koroviev began sadly, “but for him will be that ice-cold mug of beer that we, poor wanderers, so dreamed of, you and I. Our situation is sad and difficult, and I do not know what to do.”

Behemoth only spread his hands bitterly and put his cap back on his round head, overgrown with thick hair very like cat’s fur. And at that moment a quiet but commanding voice rang out above the citizen’s head:
“Let them through, Sofya Pavlovna.”

The citizen with the ledger was astonished; in the greenery of the trellis there appeared a white tailcoat shirtfront and the wedge-shaped beard of a buccaneer. He was looking affably at the two dubious ragamuffins and, what is more, making inviting gestures to them. The authority of Archibald Archibaldovich was something seriously felt in the restaurant he managed, and Sofya Pavlovna meekly asked Koroviev:
“What is your name?”
“Panayev,” he replied politely. The citizen wrote down this name and raised a questioning gaze to Behemoth.

“Skabichevsky,” the latter squeaked, for some reason pointing to his Primus. Sofya Pavlovna wrote this down too and pushed the ledger toward the visitors for them to sign it. Opposite the name “Panayev” Koroviev wrote “Skabichevsky,” and Behemoth, opposite Skabichevsky, wrote “Panayev.”

Archibald Archibaldovich, utterly astounding Sofya Pavlovna, smiling seductively, led the guests to the best table at the opposite end of the veranda, where the shade was thickest, to a table beside which the sun played merrily through one of the openings in the trellis greenery. Sofya Pavlovna, meanwhile, blinking with amazement, spent a long time studying the strange entries the unexpected visitors had made in the ledger.

Archibald Archibaldovich surprised the waiters no less than Sofya Pavlovna. He personally pulled out a chair from the table, inviting Koroviev to sit down, winked at one waiter, whispered something to another, and two waiters began bustling around the new guests, one of whom set his Primus on the floor next to his reddened boot.

At once the old tablecloth with yellow stains vanished from the table; another, whiter than a Bedouin’s burnous, flew up in the air, crackling with starch, and Archibald Archibaldovich was already whispering quietly but very expressively, bending right to Koroviev’s ear:
“What may I treat you to? I have some very special cured sturgeon... snatched it from the architects’ congress...”
“You... er... just give us some starters... er...” Koroviev lowed benevolently, sprawling on his chair.
“I understand,” Archibald Archibaldovich replied significantly, closing his eyes.

Seeing how the head of the restaurant was treating the highly dubious visitors, the waiters abandoned all doubt and set to work in earnest. One was already holding a match for Behemoth, who had taken a cigarette butt out of his pocket and stuck it in his mouth; another flew up with a clinking of green glass and set out at the places little glasses, vodka carafes and thin-walled goblets, from which Narzan is so good to drink under the awning... no, let us anticipate and say: from which Narzan used to be drunk under the awning of the unforgettable Griboyedov veranda.

“I can offer you some little fillets of hazel grouse,” Archibald Archibaldovich purred musically. The guest in the cracked pince-nez fully approved the suggestions of the brig’s commander and gazed at him graciously through his useless lens.

The fiction writer Petrakov-Sukhovei, who was dining at the next table with his wife, who was finishing a pork escalope, noticed Archibald Archibaldovich’s attentions with the powers of observation peculiar to all writers, and was very, very surprised. And his wife, a very respectable lady, was even downright jealous of the pirate on Koroviev’s account, and even tapped with her spoon... what is this, she seemed to say, why are we being kept waiting... it’s high time the ice cream was served! What’s the matter?

However, sending Madame Petrakova a seductive smile, Archibald Archibaldovich dispatched a waiter to her, but did not himself leave his dear guests. Ah, Archibald Archibaldovich was clever! And observant, too, perhaps no less than the writers themselves. Archibald Archibaldovich knew about the séance at the Variety, and about many other incidents of these days; he had heard, and, unlike others, had not let slip past his ears either the word “checkered” or the word “cat.” Archibald Archibaldovich had guessed at once who his visitors were. And having guessed, naturally, he did not quarrel with them. But that Sofya Pavlovna, what a one! Just imagine thinking up such a thing—barring the way onto the veranda to these two! But then, what can you expect of her.

Haughtily poking her spoon into her melting cream ice, Madame Petrakova watched with displeased eyes as the table in front of the two characters dressed like a pair of clowns grew, as if by magic, a crop of delicacies. Lettuce leaves washed to a shine were already sticking out of a bowl of fresh caviar... a moment, and on a separate little table specially drawn up there appeared a misted silver bucket...

Only after making sure that everything had been done with honor, only when a covered skillet, in which something was grumbling, came flying in the waiters’ hands, did Archibald Archibaldovich allow himself to leave the two mysterious visitors, and even then only after first whispering to them:
“Excuse me! Just a minute! I’ll see to the fillets personally.”

He flew away from the table and disappeared into the inner passage of the restaurant. Had some observer been able to follow Archibald Archibaldovich’s further actions, they would undoubtedly have seemed to him somewhat mysterious.

The head of the restaurant did not go to the kitchen at all to see to the fillets, but to the restaurant’s storeroom. He opened it with his own key, shut himself inside, carefully, so as not to soil his cuffs, took out of the ice chest two hefty logs of cured sturgeon, wrapped them in newspaper, neatly tied them with string and set them aside. Then in the next room he checked that his silk-lined summer coat and his hat were in their place, and only after that did he proceed to the kitchen, where the cook was diligently preparing the fillets the pirate had promised the guests.

It must be said that there was nothing strange or mysterious at all in any of Archibald Archibaldovich’s actions, and only a superficial observer could have thought them strange. Archibald Archibaldovich’s conduct followed with perfect logic from everything that had gone before. His knowledge of recent events, and chiefly Archibald Archibaldovich’s phenomenal instinct, told the head of the Griboyedov restaurant that the dinner of his two visitors, though abundant and luxurious, would be extremely brief. And the instinct that never deceived the former buccaneer did not let him down this time either.

Just as Koroviev and Behemoth were clinking their second glasses of excellent cold Moscow double-distilled vodka, the sweaty and excited newspaper reporter Boba Kandalupsky, known in Moscow for his astonishing omniscience, appeared on the veranda and at once sat down with the Petrakovs. Laying his bulging briefcase on the table, Boba immediately thrust his lips into Petrakov’s ear and began whispering some very tantalizing things into it. Madame Petrakova, languishing with curiosity, also put her ear to Boba’s plump, greasy lips. And he, glancing around furtively now and then, whispered and whispered, and individual words could be made out, such as these:
“I swear to you on my honor! On Sadovaya, on Sadovaya”—Boba lowered his voice still more—“bullets don’t touch them! Bullets... bullets... gasoline... fire... bullets...”

“Those liars who spread nasty rumors,” boomed Madame Petrakova in a contralto voice, indignantly and somewhat louder than Boba would have liked, “they are the ones who ought to be sorted out! Well, never mind, that’s how it will be, they’ll be brought to order! What pernicious fibs!”

“What do you mean, fibs, Antonida Porfiryevna!” exclaimed Boba, upset by the disbelief of the writer’s wife, and again began to whistle: “I’m telling you, bullets don’t touch them... And now there’s a fire... They go through the air... through the air...” Boba hissed, never suspecting that the very people he was talking about were sitting next to him, enjoying his whistling.

This enjoyment, however, soon came to an end. From the inner passage of the restaurant three men came swiftly out onto the veranda, their waists tightly cinched with belts, wearing leggings, with revolvers in their hands. The one in front cried out ringingly and terribly:

“Don’t move!” And at once all three opened fire on the veranda, aiming at Koroviev’s and Behemoth’s heads. Both targets instantly melted into thin air, and a pillar of fire shot from the Primus straight into the awning. Something like a gaping maw with black edges appeared in the awning and began spreading in all directions. The fire leaped through it and rose to the very roof of the Griboyedov house. Folders of papers lying on a second-floor windowsill in the editorial office suddenly flared up, then the blind caught, and here the fire, roaring as though someone were fanning it, went in pillars into the inside of the aunt’s house.

A few seconds later, along the asphalt paths leading to the cast-iron railing of the boulevard, from where, on Wednesday evening, Ivanushka had come, the first herald of misfortune, understood by no one, there now ran writers who had not finished their dinners, waiters, Sofya Pavlovna, Boba, Madame Petrakova, Petrakov.

Having stepped out in good time through a side passage, without running anywhere and without hurrying anywhere, like a captain who is obliged to leave the burning brig last, there stood the calm Archibald Archibaldovich, in his silk-lined summer coat, with two logs of cured sturgeon under his arm.

chapters.title: 29. The Fate of the Master and Margarita Is Decided
paragraphs: At sunset, high above the city, on the stone terrace of one of the most beautiful buildings in Moscow, a building constructed about a hundred and fifty years ago, there were two figures: Woland and Azazello. They could not be seen from below, from the street, since a balustrade with plaster vases and plaster flowers screened them from unwanted eyes. But they could see the city almost to its very edges.

Woland was sitting on a folding stool, dressed in his black cassock. His long, broad sword had been stuck upright between two cracked flagstones of the terrace, so that it made a sundial. The shadow of the sword was slowly and steadily lengthening, creeping toward the black shoes on Satan’s feet. Resting his sharp chin on his fist, hunched on the stool with one leg tucked under him, Woland gazed fixedly at the immense agglomeration of palaces, gigantic buildings and little hovels doomed to demolition.

Azazello, having parted with his modern outfit, that is, the jacket, the bowler hat and the patent-leather shoes, and dressed, like Woland, in black, stood motionless not far from his master, and, like him, did not take his eyes off the city.
Woland spoke:
“What an interesting city, is it not?”
Azazello stirred and answered respectfully:
“Messire, I like Rome better.”
“Yes, that is a matter of taste,” Woland replied.
After a while his voice was heard again:
“And what is that smoke over there, on the boulevard?”
“That is Griboyedov’s burning,” Azazello replied.
“One must suppose that the inseparable pair, Koroviev and Behemoth, paid a visit there?”
“There is no doubt about it whatever, messire.”

Again silence fell, and the two on the terrace watched as in the windows turned to the west, on the upper floors of the huge buildings, a broken, dazzling sun was kindled. Woland’s eye burned exactly like one of those windows, although Woland had his back to the sunset.

But here something made Woland turn away from the city and direct his attention to the round tower that stood behind him on the roof. Out of its wall stepped a gloomy man, ragged, smeared with clay, in a chiton and homemade sandals, black-bearded.
“Bah!” exclaimed Woland, looking mockingly at the newcomer. “You are the last person one would have expected here! What have you come with, uninvited but foreseen guest?”
“I have come to you, spirit of evil and lord of shadows,” the newcomer answered, glaring at Woland from under his brows in an unfriendly way.
“If you have come to me, then why did you not wish me good health, former tax collector?” Woland said sternly.
“Because I do not wish you good health,” the newcomer answered insolently.

“But you will have to reconcile yourself to it,” Woland objected, and a smile twisted his mouth. “No sooner had you appeared on the roof than you came out with an absurdity at once, and I will tell you what it is—it is in your intonation. You spoke your words as though you did not acknowledge shadows, nor evil either. Would you be so kind as to think over this question: what would your good do if evil did not exist, and what would the earth look like if the shadows disappeared from it? After all, shadows are cast by objects and people. Here is the shadow of my sword. But there are shadows of trees and of living beings. Do you want to strip the whole globe bare, sweeping away all the trees and every living thing, because of your fantasy of enjoying naked light? You are a fool.”
“I will not argue with you, old sophist,” replied Levi Matvei.
“You cannot argue with me, for the reason I have already mentioned: you are a fool,” Woland replied, and asked: “Well, speak briefly, without tiring me—why have you appeared?”
“He has sent me.”
“And what did he order you to convey, slave?”
“I am not a slave,” replied Levi Matvei, growing more and more embittered, “I am his disciple.”
“We speak different languages, you and I, as always,” responded Woland, “but the things we speak about do not change because of that. Well then?..”
“He has read the master’s work,” Levi Matvei began, “and he asks you to take the master with you and reward him with peace. Is that really hard for you to do, spirit of evil?”
“Nothing is hard for me to do,” Woland replied, “and you know that very well.” He was silent for a while and added: “But why don’t you take him to yourselves, into the light?”
“He has not earned the light, he has earned peace,” Levi said in a sorrowful voice.
“Tell him it will be done,” Woland replied, and added, his eye flaring up: “And leave me at once.”
“He asks that you also take the woman who loved him and suffered because of him,” Levi said, addressing Woland imploringly for the first time.
“We would never have thought of that without you. Go.”
Levi Matvei vanished after this, and Woland called Azazello to him and ordered him:
“Fly to them and arrange everything.”
Azazello left the terrace, and Woland remained alone.

But his solitude did not last long. The tap of footsteps and lively voices were heard on the flagstones of the terrace, and Koroviev and Behemoth appeared before Woland. But now the fat fellow did not have the Primus with him; he was loaded with other objects. Thus, under his arm he had a small landscape in a gold frame, over his arm was flung a cook’s smock, half burned, and in his other hand he held a whole salmon, skin, tail and all. Koroviev and Behemoth reeked of burning, Behemoth’s mug was covered in soot, and his cap was half burned.
“Salute, messire!” cried the irrepressible pair, and Behemoth waved the salmon.
“A fine sight you are,” said Woland.
“Messire, imagine,” Behemoth cried excitedly and joyfully, “they took me for a looter!”
“Judging by the objects you have brought,” Woland replied, glancing at the little landscape, “you are a looter.”
“Would you believe it, messire...” Behemoth began in a heartfelt voice.
“No, I would not,” Woland replied briefly.
“Messire, I swear, I made heroic attempts to save everything that could be saved, and this is all I managed to rescue.”
“You had better tell me why Griboyedov’s caught fire,” said Woland.
Both of them, Koroviev and Behemoth, spread their hands and raised their eyes to heaven, and Behemoth exclaimed:
“I cannot fathom it! We were sitting peacefully, perfectly quietly, having a bite...”
“And suddenly—bang, bang!” Koroviev took up. “Shots! Mad with fear, Behemoth and I rushed off down the boulevard, our pursuers after us, we rushed toward Timiryazev!..”
“But a sense of duty,” Behemoth put in, “overcame our shameful fear, and we went back.”
“Ah, you went back?” said Woland. “Well, then, of course, the building burned to the ground.”
“To the ground!” Koroviev confirmed mournfully. “That is, literally, messire, to the ground, as you were pleased to put it so aptly. Nothing but cinders!”

“I rushed,” Behemoth recounted, “into the meeting hall—that’s the one with the columns, messire—hoping to drag out something valuable. Ah, messire, my wife, if only I had one, would have run the risk of being left a widow twenty times over! But luckily, messire, I am not married, and I’ll tell you frankly—I am happy not to be married. Ah, messire, how can one exchange a bachelor’s freedom for a burdensome yoke!”
“Some sort of nonsense has started again,” observed Woland.

“Understood, and I continue,” replied the cat, “yes, sir, here is the little landscape. Nothing else could be carried out of the hall; the flames struck me in the face. I ran to the storeroom and saved the salmon. I ran to the kitchen and saved the smock. I consider, messire, that I did all I could, and I do not understand what accounts for the skeptical expression on your face.”
“And what was Koroviev doing while you were looting?” asked Woland.
“I was helping the firemen, messire,” replied Koroviev, pointing to his torn trousers.
“Ah, if that is so, then of course a new building will have to be built.”
“It will be built, messire,” responded Koroviev, “I venture to assure you of that.”
“Well, then, it only remains to wish that it be better than the old one,” observed Woland.
“So it will be, messire,” said Koroviev.
“You can take my word for it,” added the cat, “I am a regular prophet.”
“In any case, messire, we have arrived,” Koroviev reported, “and await your orders.”

Woland rose from his stool, went over to the balustrade, and for a long time, silent and alone, with his back turned to his retinue, gazed into the distance. Then he stepped away from the edge, sat down again on his stool and said:

“There will be no orders—you have done all you could, and for the present I have no further need of your services. You may rest. A storm will come now, the last storm; it will complete all that needs completing, and we shall set off on our way.”
“Very good, messire,” the two buffoons answered, and disappeared somewhere behind the round central tower that stood in the middle of the terrace.

The storm Woland had spoken of was already gathering on the horizon. A black cloud rose in the west and cut off half the sun. Then it covered it entirely. It grew cooler on the terrace. A little while later it became dark.

This darkness, which had come from the west, covered the enormous city. The bridges and palaces vanished. Everything disappeared, as though it had never existed in the world. A single fiery thread ran across the whole sky. Then a thunderclap shook the city. It came again, and the storm began. Woland could no longer be seen in its murk.
